841.title: Ibn Arabi's heart
841.hook: Ibn Arabi wrote that his heart had become able to take every form, in his own Sufi sense (Tarjuman al-Ashwaq 11)
841.howItsDone: Ibn Arabi's writings are studied in Sufi circles and universities alike, and this poem from the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq is often read together with his own commentary on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rumi's astrolabe: love as the instrument you look through toward its source. Your line was the astrolabe. What did your love point toward? Today, one more Sufi voice, about a heart that keeps changing shape. Day eight hundred forty-one.

Water has no shape of its own. Pour it into a cup and it's cup-shaped. Into a vase, vase-shaped. Into a cupped hand, it fits the hand. Nobody calls the water unfaithful for that. Taking the shape of what holds it is simply what water does. A Muslim mystic named Ibn Arabi, writing in Arabic, said something like that about his own heart. In a book of love poems, he wrote that his heart had become able to take every form. Today: what he meant, and how readers have heard it.
screen: `WATER HAS NO SHAPE.` → `IT FITS WHAT HOLDS IT.` → `A HEART ABLE TO TAKE EVERY FORM.`

segments.voice: First, the poem. In his collection called the Interpreter of Desires, Ibn Arabi writes, in paraphrase: my heart has become able to take every form. It is a pasture for gazelles, a cloister for monks, a temple for idols, the Kaaba of the pilgrim, the tablets of the Torah and the book of the Quran. Then: I follow the religion of love, wherever its camels turn. Second, the love poem around it. The collection is full of longing for a beloved, of ruined campsites and departing caravans, the old images of Arabic love poetry. Tradition says some readers objected that the poems were simply worldly love songs, and Ibn Arabi answered by writing a commentary on them, reading each image as a sign of divine knowledge. Third, two readings. Some readers hear the poem as saying every religion is the same. Others hear something narrower and stranger: a Muslim heart so turned toward God that it can recognize God's self-disclosure wherever it appears. This lesson doesn't choose between them. Fourth, a heart that stays open. Whatever the reading, the image is a heart that doesn't harden into one shape against the world. It stays able to receive. Like water, it takes the form of what it meets, and stays water.
screen: `THE POEM: EVERY FORM.` · `A LOVE POEM AND ITS COMMENTARY.` · `TWO READINGS.` · `A HEART THAT STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `IBN ARABI'S HEART.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a person or a place where you usually close up a little. A relative who talks politics. A neighborhood you avoid. A coworker who rubs you the wrong way. Notice what happens in your chest when you picture them. Now, without agreeing or approving, imagine your heart as water meeting that shape. It doesn't have to become them. It just doesn't have to turn to stone. Stay with that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Arabi's heart. In his love poem, a heart able to take every form, read by some as openness to all, and by others as a Muslim heart seeing God everywhere. Today's word.
Your line: able to take every form. Once today, when you feel yourself closing up, let your heart stay open just one breath longer. Day eight hundred forty-one.

what it means: a heart open enough to receive every form, heard by some as openness to all paths and by others as a Muslim heart seeing God everywhere.

842.title: Mirabai's devotion
842.hook: Hindu bhakti poets like Mirabai loved Krishna with their whole lives
842.howItsDone: Hindus practice bhakti in many ways, among them temple worship, festivals, and singing devotional songs (bhajans and kirtan), and songs attributed to Mirabai are still sung in homes and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Arabi's heart, able to take every form. Your line was able to take every form. When did your heart stay open a breath longer? That closes our Muslim and Sufi voices on love. Today, Hindu voices begin. Day eight hundred forty-two.

A woman of a royal household walks out of the palace to sing in the temple with wandering holy men. She dances in front of an image of Krishna. Her in-laws are mortified. A woman of her rank is supposed to stay behind the walls, not sing in the street with strangers. She keeps singing anyway. Her name, as the stories give it, is Mirabai, and the songs said to be hers are still sung in homes and temples. Today's word is the thing she gave her whole life to: bhakti.
screen: `A ROYAL WOMAN WALKS OUT.` → `SHE SINGS FOR KRISHNA.` → `HER NAME IS MIRABAI.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Bhakti is Sanskrit, usually translated devotion: a loving, personal turning toward God. The Bhagavad Gita uses it, where Krishna speaks of those who worship him with bhakti, and it gives its name to whole movements of poet-saints who sang their love for God in everyday languages. Second, Mirabai's story. Much of what's told about her comes from legend, and the details vary. In the stories, she gives her heart to Krishna as a child and later says he is her true husband. Her new family tries to stop her devotion. Tradition says they even sent her poison, and she drank it as an offering, and it did her no harm. Third, her songs. They speak to Krishna directly, as someone near. One refrain, in paraphrase, says: mine is Giridhar Gopal, the cowherd who lifted the mountain, and no one else. The songs are plain and intimate, full of waiting, teasing, longing, joy. They're meant to be sung, not studied. Fourth, love with a whole life. For bhakti poets, devotion isn't a feeling saved for a holy day. It reorganizes everything: where you go, whom you sit with, what you sing while you work. Some Hindus practice bhakti through temple worship and festivals, others by chanting a name of God through the day. Mirabai's story shows what that love can cost, and, in the stories, she paid it singing.
screen: `BHAKTI: LOVING DEVOTION.` · `MIRABAI'S STORY.` · `SONGS SUNG TO KRISHNA.` · `LOVE WITH A WHOLE LIFE.` · then, large: `BHAKTI.`

segments.voice: Bhakti is often sung, so today the practice uses your voice. Think of something or someone you love deeply. Choose a simple tune, any tune at all, or none. Now hum, quietly, for them. No words needed. Let the hum be the way you'd say thank you, or I miss you, or I'm glad you exist. If humming feels strange, hum anyway, softly, and notice where it vibrates in your chest. If you pray, a devotional song or name from your own tradition can take the place of the hum. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Sanskrit for loving devotion to God, the path of the poet-saints like Mirabai, who sang it with her whole life. Today's word.
Your line: devotion. Once today, give your full attention to something you love, for a few minutes, the way Mirabai sang for Krishna. Day eight hundred forty-two.

843.title: Radha and Krishna
843.hook: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda sings their love as divine love
843.howItsDone: Vaishnava Hindus worship Radha and Krishna together in temples and homes, and songs from the Gita Govinda and later devotional poets are sung in worship and danced in classical dance traditions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti, and Mirabai singing for Krishna with her whole life. Your line was devotion. What did you give your full attention to? Today, a love story those songs return to. Day eight hundred forty-three.

Night in a forest by a river. Somewhere among the trees, someone is playing a flute. In the villages nearby, the cowherd women hear it. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, they drop what they're doing and go, out into the dark, toward the sound. The flute player is Krishna, the cowherd boy his devotees worship as God. Later poets give one of the women who love him a name and a story of her own: Radha. A Sanskrit poet named Jayadeva sang their love in a long poem called the Gita Govinda. Today: Radha and Krishna, and why their love is read as divine love.
screen: `A FLUTE IN THE FOREST.` → `THE COWHERD WOMEN GO.` → `RADHA AND KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: First, the flute. In the Bhagavata Purana, the sound of Krishna's flute calls the cowherd women, the gopis, from their homes at night. Devotional readers hear the flute as God's call to the soul: a sound that makes everything else seem less urgent. Second, the quarrel. The Gita Govinda tells a love story with a hurt in the middle. In spring, Krishna dances and plays with many gopis. Radha sees, and she is wounded. She withdraws into a bower in the forest and grieves. Krishna, for his part, misses her and longs for her. A friend of Radha's goes back and forth between them carrying messages. Third, the return. At last Krishna comes to Radha, asks her pardon, and they are reunited. The poem dwells on their longing and their meeting in lush, frank detail, set among flowers, bees and moonlight. Fourth, the love as divine love. Devotional readers don't take this as only a romance. For some Vaishnava devotees, Radha is the soul longing for God, or even the very power of God's own love. Her hurt, her waiting and her reunion become a map of devotion: the ache of separation, and the joy when God comes looking. The poem is sung in worship, not only recited as literature. Some traditions emphasize the longing; others the sweetness of the meeting. Both are there in the text.
screen: `THE FLUTE CALLS.` · `RADHA IS WOUNDED.` · `KRISHNA COMES BACK.` · `THEIR LOVE AS GOD'S LOVE.` · then, large: `RADHA AND KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: If you can, put on a love song, any love song from any time or place, softly. If you can't, play one in your memory. Close your eyes and listen as if you were one of the gopis hearing the flute through the trees: not judging the song, just letting it call you. Notice what in you leans toward it. Notice the longing in it, and the sweetness. Let the song finish, then sit in the quiet after. If you pray, you can bring that longing into your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Radha and Krishna. The lovers of the Gita Govinda, whose quarrel and reunion devotees read as the soul's love for God and God's love for the soul. Today's word.
Your line: the flute. Once today, when something beautiful calls to you, a song, a voice, a view, stop for a moment and let it. Day eight hundred forty-three.

844.title: Friendly to all
844.hook: Krishna: dear to me is one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate (Bhagavad Gita 12.13)
844.howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and its twelfth chapter, on devotion, is sometimes recited on its own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Radha and Krishna, and the flute calling through the trees. Your line was the flute. What beautiful thing did you let call to you? Today, Krishna speaks again, and this time about whom he holds dear. Day eight hundred forty-four.

A battlefield, two armies facing each other, and in the space between them a chariot. The warrior Arjuna has lost his nerve, and his charioteer, Krishna, is talking him through it. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. By its twelfth chapter, Arjuna has seen a vision of Krishna's cosmic form, and now he asks a quieter question: who knows yoga better, those who worship Krishna in a form, or those who worship the formless? Krishna's answer winds toward something that isn't a ritual or a rank. It's a portrait of a person. And the portrait starts with one who hates no being. Today: friendly to all.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN ARMIES.` → `ARJUNA ASKS A QUIET QUESTION.` → `A PORTRAIT OF A PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of mine and free from ego, the same in pain and pleasure, and forgiving, that devotee is dear to me. Notice where it starts. Not with prayer, not with sacrifice. With hating no one. Second, the word friendly. In Sanskrit it's maitra. The verse doesn't say friends with all, as if everyone becomes your best friend. It says friendly: a basic warmth toward every being, the default setting of the heart. And right beside it stands compassion, karuna, which feels for those who suffer. Third, free from mine. The same verse joins friendliness to letting go of possessiveness and ego. Some readers hear a link there: unfriendliness can grow out of mine. My seat, my way, my turn. When the grip on mine loosens, there's more room to be friendly. Fourth, dear to God. Earlier in the Gita, Krishna speaks of devotion as offering. Here he says who is dear to him: the person whose love has spilled outward into how they treat every creature. Devotion to God, in this verse, shows up as friendliness to everyone else. A stranger at a bus stop becomes, in this light, part of the practice.
screen: `THE VERSE: HATING NO BEING.` · `MAITRA: FRIENDLY.` · `FREE FROM MINE.` · `DEAR TO GOD.` · then, large: `FRIENDLY TO ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a stranger you saw recently. Someone in line, a driver, a person walking a dog. You don't know their name or their story. Picture their face as well as you can. Now, gently, let yourself be friendly toward them. Not loving, not attached, just warm. The way you'd nod at a neighbor. Hold that warmth for a few breaths. Then picture passing them again tomorrow, and the nod you'd give. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Friendly to all. Krishna's portrait in the Gita of the devotee he holds dear: one who hates no being, friendly and compassionate, free from mine. Today's word.
Your line: friendly to all. Once today, be friendly to a stranger: a nod, a held door, a real thank you. Day eight hundred forty-four.

845.title: Those who love
845.hook: Guru Gobind Singh: only those who love find the Lord (Tav-Prasad Savaiye)
845.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tav-Prasad Savaiye as part of Nitnem, the daily morning prayers, and the verses are also recited when the Khalsa initiation is given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna's portrait of the devotee who is friendly to all. Your line was friendly to all. Which stranger got your nod? Today, a Sikh voice on love. Day eight hundred forty-five.

Kings on elephants hung with gold. Armies in polished armor, horses dancing. Ascetics who've stood in cold rivers and gone without food. Pilgrims who've bathed at every holy place. A Sikh hymn walks you right through a procession like that. Then, after all that spectacle, the poet stops and says, in effect: I tell you the truth, all of you, listen. Only those who love have found the Lord. The poet is Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru. Today: those who love.
screen: `KINGS ON ELEPHANTS.` → `ASCETICS IN COLD RIVERS.` → `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the hymn. The Tav-Prasad Savaiye are verses by Guru Gobind Singh, and they are part of Nitnem, the Sikh daily prayers said in the morning. The verses look at power, wealth and hard religious effort, one after another. Second, the turn. After all the display comes the line the whole hymn leans on. In the original, in the old Braj language written in Gurmukhi, it begins sach kahon, I speak the truth. Then, in paraphrase: listen, everyone, only those who have loved have found the Lord. Jin prem kio, those who loved, tin hi prabh paio, they alone found God. The word for love there is prem. Third, what the line doesn't say. It doesn't say kings and ascetics are bad. It doesn't mock pilgrimage. It says none of those, by itself, is the thing. Wealth can be held without love. Even fasting and cold baths can be done without love. The measure the Guru gives is not what you did, but whether you loved. Fourth, love that isn't soft. Guru Gobind Singh is remembered as a warrior-saint, who founded the Khalsa and stood against tyranny. So this isn't a gentle poet far from hard choices. It's a leader who knew armies firsthand, telling everyone that armies aren't what finds God. In Sikh teaching, love is the way to God, and it shows in remembering God's name, honest work and sharing with others. Today's line keeps it short: those who love.
screen: `THE HYMN AND ITS PARADE.` · `SACH KAHON: THE TURN.` · `WHAT THE LINE DOESN'T SAY.` · `LOVE THAT ISN'T SOFT.` · then, large: `THOSE WHO LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Choose one thing to love with your whole heart. A person, the breath itself, the light in the room, the simple fact of being alive. Just one. Give it everything until the bell. When your mind drifts to plans or worries, the parade going by, notice it, and come back to the one thing. No need to feel anything special. Loving here means returning. If you pray, you can bring a name of God from your own tradition into this. The bell holds the time.
Those who love. Guru Gobind Singh's line in the Tav-Prasad Savaiye: after kings, armies and ascetics, only those who love have found the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: those who love. Once today, when you're tempted to impress someone, try loving them instead. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: As a mother
846.hook: as a mother protects her only child, so cultivate boundless love for all beings (Sutta Nipata 1.8)
846.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the Metta Sutta at home and in monasteries, and some Buddhists practice metta meditation, wishing well first to themselves or loved ones and then to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Gobind Singh's line: only those who love have found the Lord. Your line was those who love. Whom did you love instead of trying to impress? Today, a Buddhist voice. Day eight hundred forty-six.

A toddler wobbles toward the edge of a pool. Across the yard, a mother is already moving, before she's even decided to. Her body knows. Nothing else in the world matters for that second. No meeting, no phone, no pride. There is one child, and she would put herself between that child and any harm. A short Buddhist text takes that instant, a fierce, protective love, and asks something startling. What if that love had no edges? Today: as a mother.
screen: `A TODDLER NEAR THE POOL.` → `A MOTHER ALREADY MOVING.` → `WHAT IF IT HAD NO EDGES?`

segments.voice: First, the image. In the Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness, the Buddha says, in paraphrase: just as a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so one should cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. The sutta reaches for a fierce, protective love and holds it up as the pattern. Second, the wish. Before that image, the sutta gives a wish, in paraphrase: may all beings be happy and at ease. Then it spells out who all means. Weak or strong, long or short, large or small, seen or unseen, near or far, born or yet to be born. Nobody is left out by size or distance, or even by not being born yet. Third, boundless. The sutta asks for this love to spread above, below and all around, without obstruction, without hatred, without enmity. The mother's love is narrow: one child. The sutta keeps its intensity and takes away the walls. That's the turn. Fourth, at all times. The sutta adds that one should keep this mindfulness whether standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake. Loving-kindness here isn't a mood for a quiet room. It's meant to go wherever the body goes. The commentaries tell that the Buddha taught it to monks who were frightened in a forest. In Theravada communities the sutta is still chanted, at home and in monasteries.
screen: `THE IMAGE: A MOTHER'S LOVE.` · `MAY ALL BEINGS BE HAPPY.` · `BOUNDLESS: NO WALLS.` · `AT ALL TIMES.` · then, large: `AS A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone you'd protect without thinking, a child, a parent, a friend, a pet. Let that warmth come clearly. Now, keeping the warmth, let the sutta's own wish move outward: may all beings be happy and at ease. First to people in this building or street. Then to people you don't know, near and far. Then to every creature, seen and unseen. Let the circle keep widening, without forcing it. If the warmth thins, return to the one you'd protect and start again. The bell holds the time.
As a mother. The Metta Sutta's pattern for loving-kindness: a mother's protective love for her only child, made boundless toward all beings. Today's word.

Your line: boundless. Once today, pick someone you'd never think to include, a face on the news, a creature underfoot, and silently wish them happy and at ease, with a little of the warmth you'd give your own. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Boundless compassion
847.hook: the second of the four boundless states in Buddhism
847.howItsDone: In Buddhist practice, compassion (karuna) is one of the four boundless states; Buddhaghosa's manual advises beginning by wishing one suffering person free of pain, then widening the wish step by step to all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, as a mother protects her only child: the Buddha's picture of love with no edges. Your line was boundless. Who did you wish well, past the people you already like? Today ends the week, and that love gets a second face. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

An ambulance goes by with its siren on. Traffic pulls over. For a few seconds, a whole street of strangers knows that someone, somewhere ahead, is having one of the worst days of their life. Some drivers say a quiet word for whoever it is. Some just feel a tug in the chest and then the light turns green. That tug has a name in Buddhism. Yesterday's love wished beings well. Today's turns toward the ones who are hurting. It's the second of four states Buddhists call boundless, and it's today's word.
screen: `A SIREN GOES BY.` → `A TUG IN THE CHEST.` → `THE SECOND BOUNDLESS STATE.`

segments.voice: First, four states with no edges. Buddhist texts name four qualities a person can grow until they reach every being: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness for others, and equanimity. In the suttas, a meditator fills the world with each one in turn, one direction after another, until the whole world is covered. Karuna, compassion, is the second. Second, what it actually is. The wish for someone to be free of their suffering. Not fixing them, not solving them. Wishing, with the whole heart, that the pain would lift. Third, its two enemies. Buddhaghosa, a Buddhist teacher, in his manual the Path of Purification, says compassion has a far enemy and a near one. The far enemy is plain: cruelty. The near enemy is sneakier. It's a sorrow that looks like compassion but sinks into its own grief, until the feeling is mostly about the one who feels it. Compassion stays turned toward the other person. Fourth, where to start. Buddhaghosa doesn't say begin with everyone. He says begin with one person you've seen in real misfortune, and let the wish grow from there: to someone dear, to someone you barely notice, and at last to someone you find hard. Boundless doesn't start boundless. It starts with one face.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now. Someone sick, someone grieving, someone you saw on the street. Keep their face in front of you. Breathing in, notice their trouble, without adding to it. Breathing out, wish them free of it. Simple words are fine: may this lift. If the feeling starts to turn into your own heaviness, come back to their face. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer from your own tradition. The bell holds the time.
Karuna. Compassion: the wish for one who suffers to be free of it, the second of the four boundless states. Today's word.

Your line: compassion. Next time a siren passes, or a hard story crosses your screen, stop for one breath and wish that person free. That ends a week of love in many voices: Ibn Arabi, Mirabai, Radha, the Gita, the Sikh hymn, the Metta Sutta, and now karuna. Day eight hundred forty-seven.
